The 18 reviews both note that the relationship appears very sensitive to local circumstances, and therefore the use of lighting in crime prevention should be context appropriate. Welsh and Farrington used a well-established methodology to combine the results of all the studies from the United States and the United Kingdom, and concluded that improved street lighting led to a “21 percent decrease in crime compared with comparable control areas.” (Welsh, 2007) The review could not determine whether these improvements were the result of situational deterrence or improved community pride and cohesion. The review concluded that improved street lighting had a larger effect on property crimes than on violent crimes, but offered no explanation for this result. More detailed research showing the effect on specific types of property crime and violent offenses is needed. 2.2.2.1.3 Specific Crime Types Based on the reviews so far on street lighting and crime, it is found that most researchers quote a figure for “total number of crimes” or “total number of calls for service” irrespective of the type; i.e., they do not analyze, for instance, crimes against the person separately from crimes against property, even though it is reasonable to believe that these types may be differently affected by the presence of lighting (Blanc, 2008). A few researchers (e.g., Quinet and Nunn, 1998) disregard certain types of crime (domestic disturbance, traffic crimes) that they regard as not being influenced by lighting. Other researchers do not give details of what types of crime are included in their analysis. None of the papers reviewed gives evidence or a causal explanation for why one type of crime or another may or may not be affected by lighting. Therefore, it is believed that existing theories of criminal behavior do not provide clarity in this area. 2.2.2.1.4 Unintended Consequences Given the different ways in which improved street lighting might affect the neighborhood where it is installed, concern arises that criminals might simply commit their crimes in nearby neighborhoods where the lighting is till poor. This phenomenon, known as spatial or geographical displacement (Clarke, 2008), might seem an obvious result of improved lighting, but related research studies showed that matters are not so simple. Displacement occurs much less often than most people, police included, assume. For example, Hesseling reviewed 55 studies of displacement undertaken and found that displacement occurred in only 22 instances (Hesseling, 1994). When it did occur, it was never complete, so that there was always a net benefit of the crime-prevention measure. Another study concluded that street offenders are much more likely to adapt their methods to the new conditions or to displace their activities to a different time of the day, rather than to offend elsewhere (Weisburd, 2006). Rather than displacement, it was also found that there is diffusion of benefits to nearby areas (same as findings in Table 4 and Table 5).
